Because the nature of a debt varies with its cause, and just as we owe God worship (religion), our parents worship (piety), and those excelling in dignity worship (observance), we owe our benefactors, from whom we received particular favors, the distinct debt of gratitude
Because gratitude only concerns financial repayment of loans
Because gratitude is a theological, not moral, virtue
P3Q106.explanation: Aquinas situates gratitude within a hierarchy of debts rooted in different causes (God, parents, those in dignity, and benefactors), each requiring a distinct virtue; gratitude addresses the debt owed specifically to a benefactor for particular favors received.

P3Q106.q: According to Aquinas, should the repayment of gratitude exceed the favor originally received?
options: No, repayment should always be exactly equal to the favor received, no more and no less

Yes, gratitude always inclines, as far as possible, to give back more than was received, since a benefactor is praised chiefly for giving gratis without obligation, and merely returning an equivalent would not itself be gratuitous
No, repayment should always be less than what was received to avoid presumption
Gratitude requires no repayment of any kind whatsoever
P3Q106.explanation: Aquinas reasons that since a benefactor deserves praise chiefly for giving freely without obligation, the recipient, to genuinely reciprocate this gratuitousness, should try to give back more than received, since merely returning the equivalent would not itself be a free gift.

P3Q107.q: According to Aquinas, what are the three ascending degrees of ingratitude, from least to most severe?
options: Ignoring a favor briefly, delaying repayment, and forgetting it entirely
Failing to repay a favor received, declining to acknowledge or express thanks for a favor, and failing entirely to recognize that a favor was received at all (including outright forgetting it)
Complaining about a gift, criticizing the giver, and returning the gift
Being poor, being sick, and being imprisoned
P3Q107.explanation: Aquinas orders the degrees of ingratitude in reverse of the order of gratitude's generation: first failing to repay, second failing to acknowledge or express thanks, and third (the worst) failing to even recognize that a favor was received.

P3Q107.q: According to Aquinas, is mere failure to repay a debt of gratitude always a mortal sin?
options: Yes, any failure of gratitude is automatically mortal

No; since the fullest debt of gratitude (a liberal, exceeding return) is not strictly obligatory, mere omission of it is usually venial, unless it involves inward contempt or withholds something the benefactor genuinely needs
No, ingratitude is never sinful in any degree
It depends entirely on the social status of the benefactor
P3Q107.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes ingratitude by mere omission (usually venial, since the debt of liberal repayment is not strictly obligatory) from ingratitude that does the opposite of gratitude, and notes that omission can become mortal if it involves contempt or withholds something genuinely needed.

P3Q108.q: According to Aquinas, under what condition is vengeance lawful rather than sinful?
options: Vengeance is always unlawful under any and all circumstances

It is lawful when the avenger's intention is directed chiefly to some good obtained through the punishment (the sinner's amendment, restraint of harm, upholding of justice, honor of God), and unlawful when the intention rests chiefly on the evil of the person punished, which belongs to hatred
Vengeance is always lawful as long as it is proportionate to the original offense
Vengeance is lawful only if carried out by the victim personally
P3Q108.explanation: Aquinas judges vengeance by the intention of the avenger: if focused chiefly on the wrongdoer's evil for its own sake, it is unlawful hatred; if directed to some genuine good achieved through the punishment, it can be lawful, provided due circumstances are observed.

P3Q108.q: According to Aquinas, can a person be justly punished for something done involuntarily, without any personal fault?
options: Never under any circumstances whatsoever

Punishment strictly as retribution requires voluntary fault, but punishment as medicine can sometimes fall on a person without personal fault in lesser (temporal) goods, for humiliation or probation, though never in spiritual goods without fault
Yes, punishment for involuntary acts is always just in every respect
Punishment for involuntary acts applies only to animals, not humans
P3Q108.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes retributive punishment (requiring voluntary fault, restoring justice's equality) from medicinal punishment (which can, without personal fault, affect lesser temporal goods for humbling or testing a person, but never spiritual goods, which are never removed without fault).

P3Q109.q: According to Aquinas, in what sense is truth a virtue, distinct from truth as a metaphysical property?
options: Truth as a virtue and truth as a metaphysical property are exactly the same thing

Truth taken as the equality between understanding/sign and the thing signified is not itself a virtue but the object of one; truth taken as the habit by which a person says what is true (truthfulness) is properly a virtue, since it makes one's act of manifestation good
Truth can never be considered a virtue under any description
Truth as a virtue applies only to mathematical and logical statements
P3Q109.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes truth as an equality (the ground of true statements, not itself a habit) from truth as truthfulness (a habit disposing a person to say what is true), and it is the latter sense in which truth is properly a virtue.

P3Q109.q: According to Aquinas, why is truth classified as a part of justice, annexed to it as a secondary virtue?
options: Because truth requires no reference to other people at all

Because truth shares two things with justice: it is directed toward another (manifestation is directed to someone else) and it establishes a kind of equality (matching outward signs to inward reality), though it falls short of justice's strict legal debt, being instead a moral debt of equity
Because truth and justice are simply identical virtues with different names
Because both truth and justice are exclusively concerned with financial transactions
P3Q109.explanation: Aquinas identifies truth's two points of contact with justice: direction toward another person and establishment of equality (between sign and reality), while noting it falls short of strict legal debt, being instead a moral debt owed out of equity.

P3Q110.q: According to Aquinas, what three elements combine to constitute the full, formal nature of a lie?
options: Wealth, power, and social status of the liar
The falsity of what is said (material element), the will to assert what is false (formal element, the essential note), and the intention to deceive (perfective element)
Public knowledge, a written record, and a court hearing
Age, gender, and profession of the speaker
P3Q110.explanation: Aquinas explains that a lie requires falsity of the statement (material), but the essential/formal element is the will to assert what one believes false, while the intention to deceive is the completing/perfective element, not the defining essence.

P3Q110.q: According to Aquinas, is every lie a sin, even a 'jocose' or 'officious' lie told for a good purpose?
options: No, only mischievous lies intended to harm are sins; jocose and officious lies are morally neutral

Yes; every lie is evil in respect of its genus because it involves signifying by words something contrary to what is in one's mind, which is unnatural and undue, though the gravity varies by the end intended (mischievous being worst, officious and jocose being lighter, sometimes only venial)
No lie is ever a sin as long as no one is harmed by it
Lies are sins only if told under oath
P3Q110.explanation: Aquinas holds that lying is evil in its very genus, since words naturally signify what is in the mind, so signifying otherwise is undue; hence every lie is a sin, though mischievous lies are gravest, and jocose/officious lies, while still sinful, are typically only venial.

P3Q111.q: According to Aquinas, is hypocrisy identical to dissimulation in general, or a narrower category?
options: They are identical in every respect with no distinction
Hypocrisy is a narrower form of dissimulation, specifically when one person simulates being another kind of person entirely, such as a sinner simulating the character of a just man
Hypocrisy has nothing to do with dissimulation at all
Dissimulation is a narrower subset of hypocrisy
P3Q111.explanation: Aquinas, following Isidore and Augustine, explains that hypocrisy is dissimulation, but not every form of dissimulation; it specifically involves simulating another person's character, as when a sinner pretends to be a just man.

P3Q111.q: According to Aquinas, is hypocrisy always a mortal sin?
options: Yes, hypocrisy is always and invariably a mortal sin with no exceptions

It depends: if a person cares nothing for actual holiness but only for appearing holy, this always implies mortal sin (total lack of holiness); but if one lacking holiness through mortal sin merely dissimulates it, the dissimulation itself is mortal only if directed to an end contrary to charity, otherwise it may be venial
No, hypocrisy is never a sin of any kind
Hypocrisy is a sin only if it involves financial fraud
P3Q111.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the hypocrite who cares only for appearing holy (always mortal sin, implying total absence of holiness) from one already in mortal sin who merely simulates the holiness he lacks, whose act of dissimulation is mortal only if its end is contrary to charity.

P3Q112.q: According to Aquinas, how does boasting (jactantia) properly relate to the virtue of truth?
options: Boasting has no relationship whatsoever to truth or falsehood
Boasting, properly speaking, is an uplifting of oneself in words above what one actually is in oneself (more properly) or above what others esteem one to be; it is opposed to truth by way of excess
Boasting is actually a form of humility taken to an extreme
Boasting concerns only claims about physical strength
P3Q112.explanation: Aquinas defines boasting as an uplifting of self through words, most properly speaking above what one is in reality (rather than merely above others' esteem), and classifies it as an excess opposed to the virtue of truth.

P3Q112.q: According to Aquinas, when is boasting a mortal sin versus a venial sin?
options: Boasting is always and invariably venial regardless of content

It is mortal when it concerns something contrary to God's glory or entails contempt/injury of one's neighbor, or when it proceeds from a mortally sinful degree of pride or vainglory; it is venial when it involves neither, such as harmless self-praise
Boasting is mortal only if done in a house of worship
Boasting can never rise to the level of mortal sin under any circumstance
P3Q112.explanation: Aquinas evaluates boasting both as a form of lying (mortal if it offends God's glory or injures a neighbor, venial otherwise) and by its cause (mortal if springing from mortally sinful pride or vainglory, especially when aimed at gain, which he considers viler still).

P3Q113.q: According to Aquinas, is all self-belittling speech classified as the sin of irony?
options: Yes, any statement diminishing oneself is automatically ironic and sinful

No; belittling oneself while safeguarding truth (concealing greater qualities but not denying what one perceives in oneself) is not irony and not sinful in itself; only belittling oneself by departing from truth (denying or disclaiming what one actually perceives to possess) constitutes irony, which is always a sin
Irony refers exclusively to sarcastic humor with no moral content
Aquinas does not discuss irony as a moral category at all
P3Q113.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes belittling oneself while preserving truth (not irony, not sinful in itself) from belittling oneself by forsaking truth, denying a quality one actually recognizes in oneself, which constitutes irony and is always sinful.

P3Q113.q: According to Aquinas, is boasting or irony generally the more grievous sin?
options: Irony is always more grievous than boasting without exception

Generally boasting is more grievous, since it typically proceeds from a viler motive (desire of gain or honor), while irony typically arises from an aversion, even if inordinate, to being disagreeable by self-exaltation; but irony can be worse when used for cunning deception
They are always exactly equal in every case
Neither irony nor boasting is ever sinful according to Aquinas
P3Q113.explanation: Aquinas, following Aristotle, generally ranks boasting as more grievous since it proceeds from baser motives like gain or honor, while irony arises from an aversion to self-exaltation; however, he notes irony can become graver when used for cunning deception.

P3Q114.q: According to Aquinas, why does friendliness (affability) qualify as a special virtue?
options: Because being pleasant to others has no moral significance at all
Because good consists in order, and it behooves man to maintain a becoming order in his mutual relations with others in deed and word, requiring a special virtue that maintains this becomingness
Because friendliness is simply a synonym for charity with no distinct content
Because friendliness applies only to relationships between family members
P3Q114.explanation: Aquinas argues that since good consists in order, and human beings need a becoming order in their mutual dealings, a special virtue, friendliness or affability, is needed to maintain this proper social order.

P3Q114.q: How does Aquinas classify friendliness/affability in relation to justice?
options: It is entirely unrelated to justice in any sense

It is a part of justice annexed to it as a secondary virtue, since like justice it is directed to another person, but it falls short of full justice because it concerns merely a debt of equity (behaving pleasantly) rather than a strict legal or favor-based debt
It is identical to justice with no distinction whatsoever
It ranks above justice as the highest of all virtues
P3Q114.explanation: Aquinas classifies friendliness as annexed to justice because, like justice, it is directed toward others, yet it falls short of the full notion of a strict debt, concerning instead the more modest debt of equitable, pleasant behavior toward those we live among.

P3Q115.q: According to Aquinas, what distinguishes mere 'complaisance' from actual flattery?
options: There is no distinction; they are the same vice under different names
One who wishes always to please others merely from that desire is 'complaisant,' while one who does so with the intention of gaining some advantage is properly called a 'flatterer' or 'adulator'
Complaisance concerns speech while flattery concerns only physical gifts
Flattery applies only to interactions with royalty
P3Q115.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the person who exceeds in pleasing others purely from desire to please (complaisant) from one who does so intending some personal gain (a flatterer or adulator), though both exceed the proper mode of friendliness.

P3Q115.q: According to Aquinas, in which three ways can flattery become a mortal sin?
options: By its matter (praising another's sin), by its intention (deceiving to injure body or soul), and by occasion (becoming, even unintentionally, an occasion of another's grave sin)
By its cost, its duration, and its location
Flattery is never a mortal sin under any circumstances
Only by praising a sin, with no other possible way it becomes mortal
P3Q115.explanation: Aquinas identifies three ways flattery is contrary to charity and thus mortal: praising another's actual sin (matter), intending to deceive and injure (intention), and inadvertently becoming an occasion for another's serious downfall (occasion).

P3Q116.q: According to Aquinas, how does quarreling differ from mere discord?
options: They are entirely identical vices

Discord arises from a lack of love uniting minds and opposes charity; quarreling arises specifically from a willingness to be disagreeable to others in speech, opposing the virtue of friendliness/affability
Discord concerns actions while quarreling concerns only thoughts
Quarreling is a synonym for physical violence, never verbal conflict
P3Q116.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes contradiction arising from lack of love for the person (discord, opposed to charity) from contradiction arising because one does not fear being disagreeable to the person addressed (quarreling, opposed to friendliness or affability).

P3Q116.q: According to Aquinas, is quarreling or flattery generally the graver sin?
options: Considered by species, quarreling is generally graver, since the virtue of friendship has a greater tendency to please than to displease, so exceeding by displeasing (quarreling) departs further from the virtue than exceeding by pleasing (flattery); but external circumstances can sometimes reverse this
Flattery is always graver than quarreling in every case with no exception
They are precisely equal in every instance without exception
Neither quarreling nor flattery is treated as sinful by Aquinas
P3Q116.explanation: Aquinas argues that since friendliness naturally tends more toward pleasing than displeasing, the quarrelsome person, who exceeds in displeasing, departs further from the virtue's nature than the flatterer; yet external motives (like deception for gain) can sometimes make flattery graver.

P3Q117.q: According to Aquinas, what is the proper matter of the virtue of liberality?
options: Physical strength and courage
Money and whatever has a money value, since it is the goods which a person's free-handedness toward others concerns
Speculative and theoretical knowledge
Sacred vessels used in the liturgy exclusively
P3Q117.explanation: Aquinas explains that liberality concerns using well the external goods one possesses, denoted by 'money,' since it belongs to the liberal man to freely part with such goods for others, unburdened by excessive attachment.

P3Q117.q: According to Aquinas, why is giving, rather than merely using money moderately on oneself, the chief act for which a liberal man is praised?
options: Because giving requires no real virtue at all

Because parting with money by giving it to others requires a greater force/virtue than spending it on oneself, similar to how throwing something farther requires more force, and virtue as such tends toward what is more perfect
Because giving is legally mandated in every case
Because keeping money always indicates greater virtue than giving it
P3Q117.explanation: Aquinas uses the analogy of throwing something farther requiring greater force to argue that parting with money by giving to others demonstrates greater virtue than spending on oneself, and virtue tends toward what is more perfect, hence giving is chiefly praised.

P3Q118.q: According to Aquinas, in what two distinct ways can covetousness manifest, corresponding to opposition against two different virtues?
options: Covetousness only ever opposes liberality and never any other virtue

Immediately, in acquiring/keeping riches unjustly (opposed to justice, e.g., theft), and interiorly, in excessive love, desire, or pleasure in riches even without unjust taking (opposed to liberality)
Covetousness manifests only through excessive spending, never through hoarding
Covetousness is entirely unrelated to any moral virtue
P3Q118.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes covetousness that unjustly acquires or retains another's property (opposed to justice, as in theft/robbery) from covetousness as inordinate interior affection for riches even without unjust taking (opposed to liberality).

P3Q118.q: According to Aquinas, why is covetousness classified as a capital vice?
options: Because it requires the most physical labor of any vice

Because riches give great promise of self-sufficiency (a condition resembling happiness, since 'all things obey money'), making covetousness, as desire for the most desirable-seeming end, a fountainhead from which many other vices spring
Because it was the first sin committed by Adam and Eve
Because only wealthy people can commit this sin
P3Q118.explanation: Aquinas explains that a capital vice gives rise to others under the aspect of a highly desirable end; since riches seem to promise self-sufficiency (resembling a condition of happiness), covetousness as desire for money becomes a capital vice from which other vices spring.

P3Q119.q: According to Aquinas, how is prodigality opposed to covetousness?
options: They are not actually opposed; they are the same vice
The covetous man loves riches excessively and exceeds in acquiring/retaining, while the prodigal is deficient in caring for riches and exceeds in giving but is deficient in retaining and acquiring
Prodigality concerns spiritual goods while covetousness concerns only physical goods
Prodigality is worse than covetousness in every possible respect
P3Q119.explanation: Aquinas explains that covetousness and prodigality are opposed in respect of excess and deficiency: the covetous man exceeds in loving, acquiring, and retaining riches, while the prodigal is deficient in valuing riches and exceeds only in giving them away.

P3Q119.q: Why does Aquinas argue that prodigality, considered in itself, is a less grievous sin than covetousness?
options: Because prodigality departs less from the opposite virtue (liberality, whose chief act is giving), because the prodigal is useful to others while the covetous man is useful to no one, and because prodigality is more easily cured, tending naturally toward the sobriety of old age and towards want
Because prodigal people are always wealthier than covetous people
Because prodigality is not actually a sin at all in Aquinas's view
Because covetous people never actually possess any money
P3Q119.explanation: Aquinas gives three reasons: giving (in which the prodigal exceeds) is closer to liberality than retaining (in which the covetous man exceeds); the prodigal benefits others while the covetous man benefits no one; and prodigality is more easily cured than the entrenched vice of covetousness.

P3Q120.q: According to Aquinas, what is the purpose of 'epikeia' (equity), and why is it a virtue?
options: Epikeia is the virtue of always following the strict letter of the law no matter the case

Because laws, framed to cover what commonly happens, can sometimes be harmful if applied to particular cases contrary to their purpose (e.g., returning a deposited sword to a madman), epikeia is the virtue of setting aside the letter of the law to follow the higher intent of justice and the common good
Epikeia concerns only ecclesiastical, never civil, law
Epikeia is simply another word for disobedience to all law
P3Q120.explanation: Aquinas explains that since laws are framed for the majority of cases and can be harmful if rigidly applied to exceptional cases (like returning a madman's sword), epikeia is the virtuous discernment to follow the deeper intent of justice rather than the letter, making it a genuine virtue.

P3Q120.q: How does Aquinas classify epikeia in relation to justice?
options: It has no relation to justice whatsoever
It is a subjective part of justice, being itself a kind of justice, and is in fact a higher rule of human action than legal justice, since legal justice is subject to its direction
It replaces justice entirely as a superior, unrelated virtue
It is a purely legal category with no moral or virtuous dimension
P3Q120.explanation: Aquinas, citing Aristotle, explains that epikeia is a kind of justice and thus a subjective part of justice; moreover, since legal justice is subject to epikeia's direction, epikeia functions as a higher rule guiding human action than mere legal justice.

P3Q121.q: According to Aquinas, why is piety counted among the Gifts of the Holy Ghost, distinct from piety as an acquired moral virtue?
options: Because the two are entirely unrelated and share nothing in common

Because the Holy Ghost moves us to a filial affection toward God as Father (the spirit of adoption), and since it belongs to piety to render duty and worship to one's father, piety as a gift is this Spirit-instigated worship and duty rendered to God as Father
Because piety as a gift concerns only reverence for civic rulers
Because gifts of the Holy Ghost cannot correspond to moral virtues in any way
P3Q121.explanation: Aquinas connects the gift of piety to the Spirit's work of adoption (Romans 8:15), whereby believers are moved to filial affection for God; since piety properly renders duty and worship to a father, the gift of piety is this Spirit-prompted worship rendered to God as Father.

P3Q121.q: According to Aquinas, how does the beatitude 'Blessed are the meek' relate to the gift of piety?
options: There is no relationship between them at all

Following one line of congruity (Augustine's ordering) it corresponds directly to piety, and even on a congruity of content, meekness has a fitting connection since it removes obstacles that would hinder acts of piety
Meekness actually opposes and undermines the gift of piety
The beatitudes have no correspondence to any of the gifts
P3Q121.explanation: Aquinas notes two ways of matching beatitudes to gifts: by order (Augustine assigns meekness to piety) and by content (where meekness fittingly relates to piety because meekness removes obstacles to acts of piety, even though a stricter content-based matching might suggest other beatitudes).

P3Q122.q: According to Aquinas, why must the precepts of the Decalogue pertain to justice?
options: Because justice is the only virtue mentioned in Scripture

Because the notion of duty essential to a precept is most evident in matters relating to another person (justice), since in matters concerning only oneself a person seems free to act as he wishes, but toward others one is manifestly obligated to render what is due
Because all Ten Commandments concern only financial transactions
Because Moses was himself a judge and thus wrote only legal precepts
P3Q122.explanation: Aquinas argues that a precept's binding character (duty) appears most evidently in matters between persons, i.e., justice, since in purely self-regarding matters one seems free, but toward others one is clearly obligated; hence the first principles of law (the Decalogue) pertain to justice.

P3Q122.q: According to Aquinas, why does the first precept of the Decalogue (against false gods) come first in the order of the Law?
options: Because it was the easiest commandment for the Israelites to understand

Because just as generation requires establishing the first (foundational) part and removing obstacles first, the Law must first lay the foundation of religion, directing the will's goodness to its true end, and first remove the chief obstacle to true religion, adherence to a false god
Because the commandments are simply listed in random order with no rationale
Because idolatry was a crime punishable only by exile, so it needed early mention
P3Q122.explanation: Aquinas draws an analogy to the order of generation (establishing the foundation first, then removing obstacles), explaining that the Law first establishes religion as foundational to the will's goodness, and its first precept removes the chief obstacle to true religion: worship of false gods.

P3Q123.q: According to Aquinas, what specific role does fortitude play among the virtues that make man's action accord with reason?
options: Fortitude rectifies reason itself, which is actually the role of the intellectual virtues

Fortitude removes the obstacle to rectitude that arises when the will is disinclined to follow reason on account of some difficulty (chiefly bodily danger), just as bodily fortitude overcomes physical obstacles
Fortitude establishes the rectitude of reason in human affairs, which is actually the role of justice
Fortitude has no distinct role and is identical to temperance
P3Q123.explanation: Aquinas explains that reason's rectitude in human affairs faces two obstacles: being drawn away by pleasure (removed by temperance) and being deterred by difficulty (removed by fortitude, which strengthens the will against the discouraging effect of danger).

P3Q123.q: According to Aquinas, why is fortitude properly and chiefly concerned with the dangers of death encountered in battle rather than other kinds of mortal danger?
options: Because fortitude concerns only physical exercise and athletic competition

Because fortitude strengthens the will against the greatest evil (death), and while other kinds of death (illness, shipwreck) do not typically come to a man through his pursuit of some good, dangers of death in battle (whether public war or private combat for justice) arise directly from pursuing a good, namely defending the common good in a just fight
Because only soldiers are capable of possessing any virtue
Because ancient Roman law required this narrow definition
P3Q123.explanation: Aquinas reasons that virtue always tends to good, and dangers of death in battle come to a person precisely through pursuing some good (defending the common good in a just war or upholding justice in a personal combat), unlike dangers from sickness or shipwreck, which do not arise from pursuing good in the same direct way.

P3Q123.q: According to Aquinas, why is 'enduring' rather than 'attacking' considered the chief act of fortitude?
options: Because attacking is always cowardly and forbidden

Because fortitude is more concerned with allaying fear than moderating daring, since danger by its nature tends to check daring but increase fear, making fear harder to overcome; enduring corresponds to repressing fear, the harder task
Because enduring requires no courage at all, unlike attacking
Because the Church forbids all forms of physical combat
P3Q123.explanation: Aquinas, following Aristotle, argues that danger naturally checks daring but increases fear, making the repression of fear (which corresponds to endurance) more difficult and thus more properly the chief act of fortitude than attacking, which corresponds to moderating daring.

P3Q124.q: According to Aquinas, why is martyrdom classified as an act of the virtue of fortitude specifically?
options: Because martyrdom requires no particular virtue at all, being purely a matter of chance

Because fortitude strengthens man in the good of virtue especially against the danger of death, and in martyrdom a person is firmly strengthened to cleave to faith and justice against the threatening danger of death inflicted through a kind of contest with persecutors, resembling a battle
Because martyrdom is exclusively an act of the virtue of religion, unrelated to fortitude
Because only soldiers who die in war can properly be called martyrs
P3Q124.explanation: Aquinas explains that fortitude strengthens the will chiefly against dangers of death, especially those occurring in a contest; since martyrdom involves standing firm in faith and justice against the danger of death imposed by persecutors, it is properly an act of fortitude, described as a kind of battle.

P3Q124.q: According to Aquinas, is death essential to the perfect notion of martyrdom, or can non-lethal suffering for the faith also count fully as martyrdom?
options: Death is not essential at all; any suffering for the faith, however minor, constitutes full martyrdom

Death is essential to the perfect notion of martyrdom, because only in losing bodily life does a person show by deed that he despises all things relating to the body for the sake of invisible goods to come; lesser hardships (imprisonment, exile) are called martyrdom only insofar as they result in death
Only death by beheading counts as true martyrdom
Martyrdom requires no suffering at all, only public declaration of faith
P3Q124.explanation: Aquinas argues that so long as bodily life remains, a person has not shown by deed that he despises all bodily goods, since men typically sacrifice possessions and even endure pain rather than lose life itself; hence the perfect notion of martyrdom requires that death actually be suffered for Christ's sake.

P3Q124.q: According to Aquinas, is faith the sole possible cause of martyrdom, or can other virtuous acts also give rise to true martyrdom?
options: Faith alone, understood narrowly as verbal profession, is the only possible cause of martyrdom

The truth of faith, which includes not only inward belief but outward profession through deeds, is the cause of martyrdom, so any virtuous deed referred to God as a profession of faith can be a cause of martyrdom, as with John the Baptist, who died not for refusing to deny the faith but for reproving adultery
Only miracles can be the cause of true martyrdom
Martyrdom can never result from any deed, only from words
P3Q124.explanation: Aquinas explains that the truth of faith includes outward profession by deeds as well as words; since virtuous deeds referred to God are professions of faith, they too can be causes of martyrdom, as shown by John the Baptist, honored as a martyr for reproving adultery rather than for refusing to renounce his faith verbally.

P3Q125.q: According to Aquinas, when does fear become sinful?
options: Fear is always sinful under every possible circumstance

Fear becomes sinful (inordinate) when the appetite shuns something that reason dictates should be endured rather than allowing the forfeiture of some greater good; when the appetite fears in accordance with what reason dictates should be shunned, it is neither inordinate nor sinful
Fear is never sinful under any circumstance whatsoever
Fear is sinful only if experienced by clergy
P3Q125.explanation: Aquinas grounds the sinfulness of fear in its being inordinate, i.e., contrary to reason's proper ordering of what to shun and what to pursue; fear that follows reason's correct dictates is not sinful, but fear that leads one to sacrifice a greater good to avoid a lesser evil is.

P3Q125.q: According to Aquinas, why is inordinate fear especially opposed to the virtue of fortitude?
options: Because fortitude has nothing to do with fear at all

Because although love, from which fear arises, and its inordinacy pervade every vice, the greatest fear of all concerns danger of death, which is fortitude's proper object; hence timidity (inordinate fear) is said to be especially, by a figure of speech, opposed to fortitude
Because fear is a purely physical sensation with no moral significance
Because only cowards are capable of experiencing fear
P3Q125.explanation: Aquinas notes that while inordinate love and fear accompany every kind of sin, the fear of death is the greatest fear and is fortitude's proper object; therefore timidity, as excessive fear of death, is specially (by antonomasia) said to be opposed to fortitude.

P3Q125.q: According to Aquinas, does fear ever excuse a person entirely from sin?
options: Fear always fully excuses every action performed under its influence

Fear excuses when one avoids a greater evil (e.g., death) by accepting a lesser one (e.g., loss of money) as reason dictates, but does not wholly excuse if one commits a greater evil (like sin) to avoid a lesser one (like bodily harm), though such an act, being mixed voluntary and involuntary, is less culpable
Fear never excuses from sin in any way whatsoever, even partially
Only physical fear, never psychological fear, has any bearing on culpability
P3Q125.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes fear that leads to accepting a lesser evil to avoid a greater one (excusable, following reason's ordering) from fear that leads to committing a greater evil, like sin, to avoid a lesser one, like bodily harm, which is not wholly excused, though culpability is diminished since acts done from fear are a mixture of voluntary and involuntary.

P3Q126.q: According to Aquinas, why does he classify fearlessness (having no fear at all of dangers) as a vice rather than a virtue?
options: Because fearlessness always indicates supreme courage and is praiseworthy in every case

Because since fear arises from love of one's own life and its due goods, and it is natural and right to love these things in due measure, having no fear at all of things that threaten them results either from a defective love (contrary to nature), from prideful presumption that one cannot be harmed, or from a defect of reason (dullness of understanding)
Because Aquinas does not actually discuss fearlessness anywhere in the Summa
Because fearlessness is identical to the virtue of fortitude with no distinction
P3Q126.explanation: Aquinas argues that since it is natural and right to love one's own life and bodily goods in due measure, a total absence of fear regarding threats to them stems either from a defective love (contrary to nature), from pride presuming immunity from harm, or from a defect of reason (as with the example of the Celts), making it a vice, though a reasoning defect may be excused if invincible.
